title: Tools for Research Data Management and curation
text:
This book collects well-documented R functions and hands-on workflows to support research data management (RDM) in practice — from ingest and validation to metadata enrichment, curation, and reporting.


How to read this book: Each chapter introduces a task area (e.g., ingest, quality control). For each function, you’ll find its purpose, arguments, return value, examples, tests, and references. Copy/paste-ready snippets are provided in callouts.







Tip



Reproducibility first. All examples rely on versioned functions in R/ with deterministic behavior and unit tests where applicable.
crumbs: 1  R Functions for Research Data Management

title: 5  Guide to opening and inspecting GeoPackage (.gpkg) files
text:
5.1 Overview
A GeoPackage (.gpkg) is an open, standards-based file format for geospatial information. It as a versatile that can hold multiple layers of vector features (points, lines, polygons), raster imagery, and even non-spatial tables. Its self-contained nature makes it an excellent format for data distribution and archival.
This document provides a guide for curators and researchers on how to programmatically inspect, read, and visualize the contents of a .gpkg file using R. It also suggests powerful external tools for deeper visual exploration.
crumbs: 5  Guide to opening and inspecting GeoPackage (.gpkg) files

Using common R functions allow us to undertand the overall structure of the data

5.3.1 Using summary() for statistical overviews
The summary() function provides a statistical summary for each column in your data frame. For numeric columns, it calculates key statistics like mean, median, and range. For text or categorical columns, it shows the length and class. It also gives a summary of the geometry column, including its type and bounding box.

file_path <- params$file_path
gpkg_data <- st_read(file_path )

5.3.4 Inspecting layers
Also, a single .gpkg file can contain many layers. Before reading any data, the first step is to inspect the file to see what it holds. The st_layers() function lists all available layers without loading them into memory.


Code
# Get the file path from the document's parameters
file_path <- params$file_path

# List all layers within the GeoPackage file
st_layers(dsn = file_path)

This is the first and most important quality check to ensure the file’s contents match its documentation.

5.4 Read a specific layer
Once the names of the layers are known, we can read a specific one into R using st_read(). This function loads the data as an sf data frame, which behaves like a regular data frame but with an extra “geometry” column that stores the spatial information.


Code
# [cite_start]Read a specific layer by name from the GeoPackage file [cite: 1]
# Note: If you omit the 'layer' argument, st_read() defaults to the first layer.
gpkg_data <- st_read(file_path, layer = "20230605_cbblackburn1_p1_labels_points") # Replace "Streams" with your layer name

title: 5  Guide to opening and inspecting GeoPackage (.gpkg) files
text:
5.5 Visualize the Data
We can create both static and interactive maps for geospacial data.

5.5.1 Static Plot
For a quick, simple preview of the geometry, the base plot() function works well.


Code
# [cite_start]Create a static plot of the layer's geometry [cite: 1]
plot(st_geometry(gpkg_data))









Code
# You can also color the plot based on a specific data column
# plot(gpkg_data["ATTRIBUTE_NAME"])




5.5.2 Interactive Map
For more compelling exploration, the leaflet package can create an interactive map that you can pan and zoom.First, the coordinates nned to be transformed to EPSG:4326 to be read by leaflet.
The leaflet package has different functions for each geometry type:

addPolygons() for areas.
addPolylines() for lines.
addCircleMarkers() or addMarkers() for points.



Code
# 1. Transform the data to the CRS that Leaflet expects (EPSG:4326)
gpkg_data_wgs84 <- st_transform(gpkg_data, crs = 4326)

# 2. Now, create the map using the *transformed* data
leaflet(gpkg_data_wgs84) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(
    radius = 3,         # Sets the circle size in pixels
    stroke = FALSE,     # Removes the circle outline
    fillOpacity = 0.8,  # Sets the transparency of the circle
    popup = ~paste0("<strong>Attribute: </strong>", as.character(gpkg_data_wgs84[[1]]))
  )




Interactive map of the data, correctly projected in WGS 84 for web display.

5.6 Additional tools
While R is excellent for programmatic analysis, other tools are indispensable for deep visual inspection and management of GeoPackage files.

5.6.1 QGIS (Desktop GIS Software)
QGIS is a free, open-source, and extremely powerful Geographic Information System. It’s the industry standard for working with geospatial data outside of a programming environment.


5.6.2 DB Browser for SQLite (Database Tool)
Since a .gpkg file is fundamentally an SQLite database, you can use a database browser to inspect its raw structure.

title: 2  Automated CSV File Checker
text:
2.1 Overview
This notebook provides a standardized procedure for checking and summarizing the contents of multiple .csv files within a directory. The goal is to automatically generate metadata summaries that can be used for data quality control, documentation, and initial exploratory analysis.
With this procedure curators can:
Assumptions:

title: 2  Automated CSV File Checker
text:
Discover files: Automatically find all .csv files in the project directory.
Extract metadata: For each file, gather information on column names, data types, and row counts.
Calculate descriptive statistics: Compute summary statistics (min, max, mean, median) and the count of missing values (NA) for each column.
Generate summary outputs: Create two final .csv files:

MetaData_CSV.csv: A detailed, long-format summary of every column from every file.
ColumnCheck_CSV.csv: A wide-format summary to easily compare column names and types across all files.




This notebook is located and run in the root directory of the data deposit.
All compressed files (e.g., .zip, .tar) have already been extracted.

2.3.2 Find CSV Files in the Selected Directory
Now that we have the path to the target directory, this code searches that location and all its subdirectories (recursive = TRUE) for files ending with the .csv extension.
We set full.names = TRUE to ensure that csv.files stores the complete file path for each file, which is necessary for the script to read them correctly.

csv.files <- list.files(
  path = target_dir,       # The directory to search
  pattern = "*.csv",       # The file pattern to look for
  recursive = TRUE,        # Search in sub-folders as well
  full.names = TRUE        # Return the full file path, not just the name
)

title: 2  Automated CSV File Checker
text:
2.4 Generate metadata summaries
Here, the code will loop through each full file path in our csv.files list, read the file, and extract the required metadata.

2.4.1 Initializing the summary table

csv.summ <- data.frame(
  file.name = character(),
  column.name = character(),
  column.type = character(),
  rows = integer(),
  min = character(),
  mean = character(),
  med = character(),
  max = character(),
  NAs = character()
)



2.4.2 Processing each file
Here, we systematically loops through each CSV file selected to summarize the data and handle errors. For valid data, we extract metadata (like column names, data types, and row count), and calculate descriptive statistics (min, mean, max, and a count of missing values). When not valid columns are found (corrupted or contains unexpected data types) the script print a detailed message in the console identifying the problematic file and the specific error.

# The Main Loop: Processing Each File
for (i in csv.files) {
  
  # Use tryCatch to handle potential errors in a file without stopping the whole script
  tryCatch({
    
    # --- All the original processing code is placed inside the tryCatch block ---
    tmp <- read.csv(i)
    
    tmp.meta <- data.frame(
      file.name = basename(i),
      column.name = colnames(tmp),
      column.type = sapply(tmp, class),
      rows = nrow(tmp)
    )
    
    tmp.stat <- tmp %>%
      summarise(
        across(
          .cols = everything(),
          .fns = list(
            min = ~min(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
            med = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
            max = ~max(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
            NAs = ~sum(is.na(.x))
          ),
          .names = "{.col}|{.fn}"
        )
      ) %>%
      mutate(
        across(everything(), as.character)
      ) %>%
      pivot_longer(
        cols = everything(),
        names_to = c("column.name", ".value"),
        names_pattern = "(.*)\\|(.*)"
      )
      
    tmp.meta <- full_join(tmp.meta, tmp.stat, by = "column.name")
    
    csv.summ <- bind_rows(csv.summ, tmp.meta)
    
  }, error = function(e) {
    # If an error occurs for a file, this code will run instead of crashing
    message(paste("--- ERROR --- Failed to process file:", i))
    message(paste("Specific error message:", e$message))
    message("Skipping this file and continuing with the next one.\n")
  })
}

# Clean up temporary variables from the loop
rm(tmp, tmp.stat, tmp.meta)

section: 3.5 Extract extensions and generate summary table
text:
3.5 Extract extensions and generate summary table
The code takes the complete list of file paths and performs two steps:

Extract extensions: It isolates the file extension from each path. The logic is designed to handle files with multiple dots (e.g., archive.tar.gz) and files with no extension at all.
Count and summarize: It then counts the occurrences of each unique extension and sorts the results to show the most common file types first.



Code
file_summary <- tibble(FilePath = all_files) %>%
  mutate(
    # basename() gets just the filename from the full path
    FileName = basename(FilePath),
    # Use stringr for a more readable and robust extraction
    Extension = str_extract(FileName, "(?<=\\.)[^.]+$") %>%
      # If no extension is found (returns NA), replace with a descriptor
      replace_na("(no extension)")
  ) %>%
  count(Extension, name = "Count", sort = TRUE)

print("--- Summary of File Extensions ---")

3.6 Additional tools

3.6.1 Identify Unexpected Formats
Quickly scan the Extension column. Do you see any proprietary formats (.xlsx, .psd, .paj) that should have been converted to open, preservation-friendly formats (.csv, .tiff, .txt)?


3.6.2 Find and Remove System “Junk” Files
Many operating systems create hidden files that are not part of the actual dataset and should be removed before publication.
Common examples to look for: * DS_Store (macOS) * Thumbs.db (Windows) * __MACOSX (Created by macOS when zipping files) * .Rhistory or .Rproj.user (RStudio project files)
If these appear in your summary, you can locate and delete them to clean the dataset.
